questions.learningObjective: Apply intelligent agents to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a agent reports the measured quantity. With 7 and 2 as the stated parameters, a performance measure awards +7 points for each correctly filed document, subtracts 2 for each misfiled document, and subtracts 3 for each second of delay. An agent files 4 documents correctly, misfiles 1, and finishes in 4 seconds. What total score does the performance measure assign to this behavior?

options.misconception: Adds the misplacement penalty rather than subtracting it
Counts misplaced items as if they were correctly sorted
Treats delay cost as a reward instead of a penalty

questions.explanation: The measure sums three signed contributions: +7 times 4 correctly filed documents gives 28, minus 2 times 1 misfiles gives -2, and minus 3 times 4 seconds gives -12. The total 28 - 2 - 12 = 14 rewards correctness and penalizes both errors and delay. Adding the delay term, adding the misfiles, or crediting misfiles as correct all invert the intended penalties, so those totals are wrong.
questions.hint: Write each contribution with its sign, then add the three products.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply problem formulation to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: For problem formulation, illustration 3402: a cleaning robot maps a room but cannot observe furniture that family members move after it looks away. Its wheel commands have perfectly predictable effects, yet the room layout keeps changing while it works and positions vary over a continuum. Which set of environment properties best characterizes this task? Use the information provided.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
Partially observable, stochastic, static, continuous.
options.misconception: Mistakes unseen changes for random action outcomes.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, static, discrete.
options.misconception: Ignores both passing time and continuous positions.

options.text: Fully observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
options.misconception: Wrongly grants the agent complete state information.

questions.explanation: The robot cannot see every relevant fact, so the environment is partially observable. Actions have perfectly predictable effects, so it is deterministic. The layout changes while the agent deliberates, so it is dynamic. Positions range over a continuum, so it is continuous. Each competing option flips one of these four properties and therefore misdescribes the task.
questions.hint: Check observability, action predictability, change over time, and whether the state space is discrete.

questions.learningObjective: Apply agent designs to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: For agent designs, illustration 3403: an agent selects each action using only the percept it receives at this instant. It keeps no record of earlier observations and builds no model of how the environment evolves. Which agent design does this description match? Use the information provided.

options.text: A simple reflex agent acting only on the current percept.
A goal-based agent planning toward a target state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes explicit goals and lookahead search.

options.text: A utility-based agent maximizing expected satisfaction.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes a utility function over outcomes.

options.text: A model-based reflex agent tracking hidden state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the agent maintains any state at all.

questions.explanation: A simple reflex agent maps the current percept directly to an action through condition-action rules, with no memory or world model. The description explicitly denies stored history and an environment model, ruling out model-based, goal-based, and utility-based designs, each of which needs internal state beyond the present percept.
questions.hint: Ask whether the agent stores anything beyond the percept in front of it.

questions.stem: Working from 0, 5, and 3, on a four-connected grid an agent starts at (0, 0) and must reach a goal at (5, 3). Each unit step costs 1 and no obstacles are present. What is the Manhattan-distance heuristic value at the starting state?

options.misconception: Uses the area of the rectangle instead of step distance
Counts only the larger coordinate displacement
Undercounts by assuming the goal square needs no move

questions.explanation: Manhattan distance adds the absolute coordinate differences: |5 - 0| + |3 - 0| = 5 + 3 = 8. Because there are no diagonal moves, this is also the exact optimal path cost. Multiplying coordinates, dropping one step, or keeping only the larger displacement each fails to sum both coordinate gaps and so understates the distance.

questions.stem: Working from 4, 2, and 5, a two-ply game tree has a MAX root with two MIN children. The first MIN child has leaves 4 and 2; the second MIN child has leaves 2 and 5. Under minimax with both players choosing optimally, what value is backed up to the root?

options.misconception: Assumes MAX gets to pick a leaf directly
Assumes MIN chooses at the root
Swaps the roles of MAX and MIN at the two levels

questions.explanation: Minimax backs up values from the leaves. Each MIN child takes the smaller of its leaves, giving 2 and 2. The MAX root then takes the larger of those, 2. Taking maxima at the MIN level swaps the players, while taking a global maximum or minimum ignores the alternating levels entirely, so each of those answers misapplies the recurrence.

questions.learningObjective: Apply informed search to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a agent computes this result. The informed search question: a heuristic h satisfies h(n) <= h*(n) for every state n, where h*(n) is the true optimal cost from n to a goal. Which property does h necessarily have? Use the information provided.

options.text: Admissible: it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.
Monotone: its value never decreases along a path.
options.misconception: Wrongly states the opposite of the usual monotonicity direction.

options.text: Optimal: it guarantees the best path without any search.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims a bound alone searches the space.

options.text: Consistent: it obeys the triangle inequality on every arc.
options.misconception: Wrongly names the stronger arcwise condition.

questions.explanation: The inequality h(n) <= h*(n) is exactly the definition of admissibility: the estimate never overestimates the remaining cost. Consistency is a stronger condition involving arc costs between neighboring states, and a heuristic being admissible does not by itself make search instantaneous or optimal without the surrounding algorithm guarantees. The competing options name different or invented properties.
questions.hint: Compare the estimate to the true remaining cost, not to neighbor costs.

questions.learningObjective: Apply bayesian inference to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Using 0.08 together with 0.74 and 0.73, a disease has prevalence 0.08. A test detects it with sensitivity 0.74 when present and has specificity 0.73 when absent. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to four decimals, that this person actually has the disease?

options.misconception: Reports the prior probability of disease
Reports only the joint numerator, unnormalized
Reports sensitivity and ignores the base rate

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives P(D|+) = se*p / (se*p + (1 - sp)*(1 - p)) = 0.059 / (0.059 + 0.248) = 0.1925. The numerator alone is not a probability because it is unnormalized, and the sensitivity or the prior each ignore the false-positive contributions and the base rate, which is precisely the base-rate fallacy.
questions.hint: Compute true positives and false positives over a population, then take the true-positive share.

questions.stem: Using 0.4 together with 0.3 and 0.1, in a Bayesian network with edge A -> B, the prior is P(A) = 0.4. The conditional table gives P(B | A) = 0.3 and P(B | not A) = 0.1. What is the joint probability P(A and B), to four decimals? Give the exact answer, showing the key step.

options.misconception: Computes the marginal probability of the child instead
Reports the conditional probability and ignores the parent
Uses the conditional probability of the wrong parent state

questions.explanation: The joint distribution factorizes as P(A, B) = P(A) * P(B | A) = 0.4 * 0.3 = 0.12. Adding the contribution from not A computes the marginal P(B), and using P(B | not A) or the conditional alone does not follow the factorization for the event A and B together.
questions.hint: Multiply the parent's prior by the child's conditional given that parent state.

questions.stem: On propositional logic, given the truth assignment P = false, Q = false, R = false, evaluate the propositional formula (P and Q) or (not P and R). Which statement is correct? Give the exact answer, carefully.

options.text: False, because neither disjunct holds.
True, but only when R is false.
options.misconception: Wrongly ties the value to R rather than to the disjuncts.

options.text: Undetermined without knowing Q and R together.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims the truth value cannot be evaluated.

options.text: True, because at least one disjunct holds.
options.misconception: Reverses the truth value of the disjunction.

The disjunction of false and false is false, so neither disjunct holds. The alternatives either invert the result or wrongly claim the value is undecidable when all atoms are assigned.
questions.hint: Evaluate each conjunction first, then combine them with or.

Ignores the learning rate entirely
Performs gradient ascent by flipping the update sign

Adding the gradient instead ascends the loss, dropping the factor of two uses the wrong derivative, and omitting the learning rate takes a full-size step, so each alternative is a distinct calculus or step-size error.

questions.stem: A regressor predicts 4, 2, 2 for three examples whose true targets are 5, 1, 6. What is the mean squared error of these predictions, to four decimals?

Corrupts the first residual by adding instead of subtracting
Uses mean absolute error instead of squared error

Mean absolute error squares nothing, skipping the division reports the total rather than the mean, and adding in any residual uses the wrong sign, so those values are not the MSE.

questions.stem: A classifier's confusion matrix reports 20 true positives, 3 false positives, and 2 false negatives. What is the F1 score for the positive class, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports recall and ignores precision
Uses a simplified accuracy that drops true negatives
Reports precision and ignores recall

questions.hint: Compute precision and recall, then take their harmonic mean.

Multiplies the features instead of weighting them
Omits the intercept term from the prediction

questions.stem: In the synthetic sampling procedure below, a model produces the following output. A logistic regression model computes a logit of z = -1 for a given input. What is the predicted probability of the positive class, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, precisely.

Reports the complement probability of the positive class
Flips the exponent sign, inverting the sigmoid

questions.stem: On the figures 0.4, 0.3, 0.1, a naive Bayes classifier has class prior 0.4. Given two observed features, the class-conditional likelihoods for the positive class are 0.3 and 0.3, and for the negative class they are 0.3 and 0.1. options.misconception: Uses a single likelihood and ignores the other evidence
Reports the prior and ignores the observed features
Reports the unnormalized numerator as if it were a posterior

Computes entropy instead of Gini impurity
Reports purity, the complement of Gini impurity

questions.stem: A bipolar perceptron has weights w1 = 4, w2 = 5 and bias 2. For inputs x1 = 3, x2 = 2, it outputs +1 when the weighted sum is nonnegative and -1 otherwise. What is its output?

Flips the sign of the step function output
Reports the weighted sum, not the thresholded output

questions.explanation: The weighted sum is 4(3) + 5(2) + 2 = 24. Since 24 is nonnegative, the bipolar step outputs 1. Flipping the sign misstates the step, zero belongs to a binary step, and the raw sum skips thresholding entirely.

questions.stem: Given the figures 9, 12, 0.99, in a Q-learning update, taking action a in state s yields an immediate reward of 9 and leads to state s'. From s' the best action has Q-value 12 (the two successor Q-values are 9 and 12), and the discount factor is gamma = 0.99. What is the target value r + gamma * max Q(s', a'), to four decimals?

options.misconception: Forgets to discount the future value
Uses the first successor value instead of the maximum
Sums successor values instead of taking the maximum

Using one successor value ignores the maximization, dropping the discount fails to reduce future rewards, and summing successors double-counts the future. The Bellman optimality target requires exactly the maximum of the successor values.
questions.hint: Take the largest successor Q-value, discount it, and add the immediate reward.

What is the most likely flaw in this procedure? Use the information provided, using only the information above.

options.misconception: Wrongly diagnoses label skew, which is not described.

options.misconception: Wrongly attributes the issue to training duration.

questions.stem: In the synthetic sampling procedure below, a learner computes this result. Turning to decision thresholds: a probabilistic classifier outputs a score for the positive class. If the decision threshold for predicting positive is raised while the model and data stay fixed, what generally happens to recall and precision? Use the information provided, using only the information above.

options.text: Recall rises while precision tends to fall.
options.misconception: Describes the effect of lowering, not raising, the threshold.

options.text: Both precision and recall rise together.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the two metrics move in the same direction.

options.text: Neither metric changes with the threshold.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes threshold and metrics are independent.

options.text: Recall falls while precision tends to rise.

Treats delay cost as a reward instead of a penalty
Adds the misplacement penalty rather than subtracting it

options.misconception: Ignores both passing time and continuous positions.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
Fully observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
options.misconception: Wrongly grants the agent complete state information.

options.misconception: Mistakes unseen changes for random action outcomes.

Undercounts by assuming the goal square needs no move
Uses the area of the rectangle instead of step distance

Swaps the roles of MAX and MIN at the two levels
Assumes MAX gets to pick a leaf directly

questions.explanation: Minimax backs up values from the leaves. Each MIN child takes the smaller of its leaves, giving 4 and 2. The MAX root then takes the larger of those, 4. questions.stem: For the informed search case numbered 3474, a heuristic h satisfies h(n) <= h*(n) for every state n, where h*(n) is the true optimal cost from n to a goal. Which property does h necessarily have? Use the information provided, showing the key step.

options.misconception: Wrongly claims a bound alone searches the space.

options.text: Admissible: it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.
Consistent: it obeys the triangle inequality on every arc.
options.misconception: Wrongly names the stronger arcwise condition.

options.text: Monotone: its value never decreases along a path.
options.misconception: Wrongly states the opposite of the usual monotonicity direction.

questions.stem: The case uses 0.18, 0.79 and 0.93; a disease has prevalence 0.18. A test detects it with sensitivity 0.79 when present and has specificity 0.93 when absent. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to four decimals, that this person actually has the disease?

options.misconception: Reports only the joint numerator, unnormalized
Reports sensitivity and ignores the base rate
Reports the prior probability of disease

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives P(D|+) = se*p / (se*p + (1 - sp)*(1 - p)) = 0.142 / (0.142 + 0.057) = 0.7124. The numerator alone is not a probability because it is unnormalized, and the sensitivity or the prior each ignore the false-positive contributions and the base rate, which is precisely the base-rate fallacy.
questions.hint: Compute true positives and false positives over a population, then take the true-positive share.

Counting gives class 1 with 4 votes, the largest share. k-NN does not weight distant neighbors more heavily, does not invent absent classes, and here the vote is not tied, so the competing answers misapply the voting rule.
questions.hint: Count the labels among all k nearest neighbors and take the plurality.

questions.learningObjective: Apply naive bayes to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: The numbers 0.8 and 0.4 with 0.1 apply here; a naive Bayes classifier has class prior 0.8. Given two observed features, the class-conditional likelihoods for the positive class are 0.4 and 0.8, and for the negative class they are 0.1 and 0.5. What is the posterior probability of the positive class, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports the prior and ignores the observed features
Reports the unnormalized numerator as if it were a posterior
Uses a single likelihood and ignores the other evidence

questions.explanation: Naive Bayes multiplies likelihoods under the conditional-independence assumption: the positive score is 0.8*0.4*0.8 = 0.256 and the negative score is (1-0.8)*0.1*0.5 = 0.01. Normalizing gives 0.9624. The numerator alone is not normalized, one likelihood discards evidence, and the prior ignores the features entirely.
questions.hint: Multiply each class's prior by its likelihoods, then normalize across classes.

questions.stem: The numbers 12 and 5 apply here; a decision-tree leaf contains 12 examples of one class and 5 of the other. What is the Gini impurity of this leaf, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

Reports purity, the complement of Gini impurity
Uses only the majority fraction, not squared shares

Reports half the margin, forgetting the factor of two
Reports the weight norm instead of the margin width

Uses the median rather than the k-means mean
Uses the maximum instead of the centroid mean

questions.stem: A PCA fit reports eigenvalues 43, 17, and 10 for the first three principal components. What fraction of the total variance is explained by the first principal component alone, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports the raw eigenvalue, not a fraction of variance
Divides by one eigenvalue instead of the total variance
Reports the variance of the first two components combined

questions.explanation: The proportion of variance explained by a component is its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues. The total is 43 + 17 + 10 = 70, so the first component explains 43/70 = 0.6143. Using one eigenvalue as the denominator, combining two components, or reporting the raw eigenvalue does not give the fraction for the first component alone.

options.misconception: Adds a spurious five to the support of A
Divides by a made-up transaction total rather than support of A
Inverts the numerator and denominator

questions.explanation: Confidence of A -> B is support(A and B) / support(A) = 30/39 = 0.7692. It measures how often B occurs among transactions containing A. questions.stem: A bipolar perceptron has weights w1 = 5, w2 = -1 and bias 2. For inputs x1 = -2, x2 = 3, it outputs +1 when the weighted sum is nonnegative and -1 otherwise. What is its output?

options.misconception: Reports the weighted sum, not the thresholded output
Flips the sign of the step function output
Uses a binary zero/one step instead of the bipolar step

questions.explanation: The weighted sum is 5(-2) + -1(3) + 2 = -11. Since -11 is negative, the bipolar step outputs -1. Flipping the sign misstates the step, zero belongs to a binary step, and the raw sum skips thresholding entirely.

Omits the bias connections to each unit
Adds rather than multiplies inputs and units

Ignores the zero-padding term
Assumes unit stride and no padding

questions.learningObjective: Apply value functions to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Using 10 together with 11 and 3, in a Q-learning update, taking action a in state s yields an immediate reward of 10 and leads to state s'. From s' the best action has Q-value 11 (the two successor Q-values are 11 and 3), and the discount factor is gamma = 0.9. What is the target value r + gamma * max Q(s', a'), to four decimals?

options.misconception: Sums successor values instead of taking the maximum
Uses the first successor value instead of the maximum
Forgets to discount the future value

questions.explanation: The one-step target is r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') = 10 + 0.9 * 11 = 19.9. Using one successor value ignores the maximization, dropping the discount fails to reduce future rewards, and summing successors double-counts the future. The Bellman optimality target requires exactly the maximum of the successor values.
questions.hint: Take the largest successor Q-value, discount it, and add the immediate reward.

Sums rewards with no discounting
Drops the third reward entirely

Summing without discount treats future rewards as equal to immediate ones, dropping the last term truncates the horizon, and applying gamma to the first reward discounts the immediate reward, which the definition does not do.

Uses a base-ten logarithm instead of the natural logarithm
Reports inverse document frequency alone, ignoring term frequency

Normalizes raw scores instead of exponentiating them
Reports the unnormalized exponential

questions.stem: In the synthetic sampling procedure below, a system yields these values. From the inputs 0.9, 0.4, a binary classifier selects group A at rate 0.9 and group B at rate 0.4. options.misconception: Adds the rates instead of taking their difference
Reports the ratio of rates instead of their difference
Multiplies the two rates rather than differencing them

questions.explanation: Demographic parity difference is the absolute gap in positive selection rates: |0.9 - 0.4| = 0.5.
